About nine to ten times their yearly profit. That number is the multiple. Lane makes eleven million a year, so that gives us ninety-nine to a hundred and ten million.
So Mark is offering about eight times. Is my company undervalued?

Hi Eduarda, it's James. Quick notes for your call with Victor on Friday. Keep it simple. Victor doesn't need the spreadsheet. He needs a story that he can repeat to his family. Start with the comparables: the three packaging deals from last year, all between nine and ten times profit. Then give him the ballpark figure, around a hundred million. Don't talk about the discount rate unless he asks. If he asks, tell him we used ten percent, which is normal for a stable company like Lane. And remind him that NorthPack needs his factories, so a premium is realistic. Call me after.

There are three common ways to value a company. The first is comparables: you look at similar companies and at what buyers paid for them. The second is the multiple. You take the company's yearly profit and multiply it by a number, usually between six and twelve, depending on the sector. The third is discounted cash flow, or DCF. Here you estimate the money that the company will make in the future, and you use a discount rate to bring it back to today's value. No method is perfect. That is why bankers use all three and present a range, not one exact number. When you explain a valuation to a client, start with the range, and then explain the method that the client trusts most.

Victor called Eduarda because he did not understand Mark's offer. First, Eduarda explained the comparables, which were three packaging companies sold last year. Then she showed him the multiple: nine to ten times Lane's profit. Next, she explained that the cash flow model gave a similar ballpark figure. Victor understood that his company was undervalued at ninety million. In the end, they decided to go back to Mark with one hundred and five million.
